keyVerseText: I am the LORD your God, which brought you forth out of the land of Egypt, that ye should not be their bondmen; and I have broken the bands of your yoke, and made you go upright.
rootMeaning: The root of קוֹמְמִיּוּת (qôwmᵉmîyûwth) is קוּם (qûwm), which carries the fundamental sense of rising up, standing, or establishing. This root encompasses a broad range of actions associated with lifting, enduring, confirming, and setting upright. Thus, the noun קוֹמְמִיּוּת conveys not merely a static posture but an active state of being raised or established upright. This etymological background enriches the English gloss 'upright' by implying both physical elevation and a sustained, confirmed position of dignity or freedom.
usageInScripture: This term appears only once in the Hebrew Scriptures, specifically in Leviticus 26:13, where it is translated as 'upright.' Its singular occurrence limits the range of translation, but the consistent rendering as 'upright' highlights the concept of standing or walking with dignity and freedom. The adverbial use in this verse underscores a manner of going or living that is marked by uprightness, revealing a figurative extension from physical posture to a state of liberty and honor.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding קוֹמְמִיּוּת in its original sense deepens our appreciation of God's redemptive work. The idea of being made to go 'upright' reflects God's deliverance of His people from bondage, not only physically but also morally and spiritually. It signifies a restored standing before God, a life elevated from slavery to freedom, and a walk characterized by dignity under His covenant. For the Christian believer, this word resonates with the new life in Christ, who lifts us up from the bondage of sin to walk uprightly before God, empowered by grace and truth.
keyVerseReflection: Leviticus 26:13 declares, 'I am the LORD your God, which brought you forth out of the land of Egypt, that ye should not be their bondmen; and I have broken the bands of your yoke, and made you go upright.' Here, קוֹמְמִיּוּת captures the transformative effect of God's deliverance—He not only frees His people but also enables them to walk in freedom with dignity and honor. The word emphasizes the active, ongoing nature of this uprightness, portraying a life established by God's power rather than mere release from oppression.
